pr_body:
Fix #102788. This implementation differs somewhat compared to the [stj-schema-mapper](https://github.com/eiriktsarpalis/stj-schema-mapper) prototype in a few ways:

1. Nullable-oblivious reference types are always reported as nullable (this is controlled by a flag in the prototype).
2. The `OnSchemaNodeGenerated` callback is invoked for `$ref` schemas.
3. `$ref` schemas are only being generated for recursive types.
4. `{ }` and `{"not": true }` node schemas are normalized into `true` and `false` respectively.

issue_context.title: [API Proposal]: Add a JSON schema exporting component for STJ contracts
comments:
Tagging subscribers to this area: @dotnet/area-system-text-json, @gregsdennis
See info in [area-owners.md](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/area-owners.md) if you want to be subscribed.

As a maintainer of the JSON Schema specification, I'm very interested in the mapping between types and their constituents and the schemas that are generated.  I consider this mapping part of the API.  I would like to suggest very limited functionality (just obvious stuff, like what you show in your example) to start.  I recommend steering away from defining edge cases.

We have a [project](https://github.com/json-schema-org/vocab-idl) in JSON Schema that seeks to define that mapping in a language-agnostic way.  While there are plenty of generators ([codegen](https://json-schema.org/implementations#from-code) / [schemagen](https://json-schema.org/implementations#generators-from-schemas)), so far none of these have jumped in to help define these rules, instead merely adding to the pool of non-interoperability by doing what makes sense to them.  I'd love for this effort to contribute back into our project to help define the mapping between JSON Schema and types.

What I'd like to see out of this effort is a beginning toward generating a schema from a type, then being able to take that schema and generate equivalent types in other languages.

---

As a .Net developer, I understand that this isn't the final vision for JSON Schema provided by .Net.  As such, I wonder where this fits in the future when the final vision (whatever that ends up being) is realized.  Will these types and methods still be available?  Are we comfortable with this existing alongside some potential dedicated JSON Schema model?

Specific notes about API:

### `JsonSchemaExporterCompatibilityMode`

"Strict" has a different meaning in a JSON Schema context than what's listed in the comment.  For JSON Schema, "strict" generally means that only the declared properties are allowed, i.e. the schema contains `additionalProperties: false`.  (This also has a side effect of not being able to use the schema as a "base type".)

Also be aware that declaring a property with `type: null` means that the property is present with a `null` value.  It has no effect if the property doesn't exist in the instance.  It seems that having `Strict` (allowing null property values) as the default is in conflict with the serializer's default behavior of skipping properties with `default` values.

### `AllowSchemaReferences`

I'm curious how generation works when setting this false and trying to generate for a recursive structure or some other circumstance that _requires_ a `$ref`.

In my generation lib, I found that a lot of cases required that I have optimization (collecting similar types into `$defs`) enabled.

### `ParentCollection`

Why have this separate from the type to generate for?  `List<T>` is generally quite different from `T`.

> I'm very interested in the mapping between types and their constituents and the schemas that are generated. I consider this mapping part of the API. I would like to suggest very limited functionality (just obvious stuff, like what you show in your example) to start. I recommend steering away from defining edge cases.

To clarify, this is not a .NET type to JSON schema mapping component, it is an STJ contract (aka `JsonTypeInfo`) to JSON schema mapping component. As such it neither exactly corresponds to the shape of a type (e.g. because of the presence of attributes, custom converters, user-defined contracts or other known STJ quirks) nor is it responsible for driving the contract derivation logic. That responsibility solely sits with whatever `IJsonTypeInfoResolver` you are using, and the schema exporter's responsibility would be to provide a faithful and complete mapping of the contracts to a rudimentary schema document. The general principle is that whatever JSON is produced from or accepted by a particular `JsonTypeInfo` should be valid under the schema exported from that same `JsonTypeInfo`.

> I'd love for this effort to contribute back into our project to help define the mapping between JSON Schema and types.
>
> What I'd like to see out of this effort is a beginning toward generating a schema from a type, then being able to take that schema and generate equivalent types in other languages.

I'm a firm believer of schema-first approaches, namely using schemas to generate types and not the other way around. Code-first largely relies on convention and can be imprecise because not all type system concepts have first-class representation or are relevant in a particular schematization format. I realize I'm stating this in an API proposal that caters to code-first scenaria (still a huge deal in .NET!), however longer-term I would personally place my bets on schema-first.

> As a .Net developer, I understand that this isn't the final vision for JSON Schema provided by .Net. As such, I wonder where this fits in the future when the final vision (whatever that ends up being) is realized. Will these types and methods still be available? Are we comfortable with this existing alongside some potential dedicated JSON Schema model?

Longer term, we need an exchange type that offers basic validation and keyword extensibility. I've purposely designed the proposal so that corresponding APIs targeting the exchange type can be added in the future by qualifying method names with "Node", e.g. "GetJsonSchemaAs**Node**" and "OnSchema**Node**Generated".

> It seems that having Strict (allowing null property values) as the default is in conflict with the serializer's default behavior of skipping properties with default values.

That's changing in .NET 9 (for properties at least). We stopped short of making it the default behaviour for fear of breaking changes, but given that this is a new component we have the luxury of being more deliberate about the desirable behaviour.

> I'm curious how generation works when setting this false and trying to generate for a recursive structure or some other circumstance that requires a $ref.

Similar to the serializer, it will throw an exception if the `JsonSerializerOptions.MaxDepth` value is reached.

> Why have this separate from the type to generate for? List<T> is generally quite different from T.

It provides context when visiting the schema for `T` that it is being generated as an element for `List<T>`. Users can use that information to, say extract attribute annotations from the parent collection or make other modifications to the schema document.

> To clarify, this is not a .NET type to JSON schema mapping component, it is an STJ contract (aka JsonTypeInfo) to JSON schema mapping component.

This is a nuance. I think most people are going to see/use it as generating a schema from a type; it just has to go through the STJ source generator a little, which kinda makes sense because it's a _JSON_ schema.  I doubt (public) users will really see the difference.

Regardless, there's still some underlying logic that dictates what kinds of .Net constructions yield what kinds of schema constructions.  That's what the IDL vocab project (basically me) is interested in.

> I'm a firm believer of schema-first approaches, namely using schemas to generate types and not the other way around.

I'm excited to see this take hold across .Net! (cc: @markrendle / @mwadams)

> I've purposely designed the proposal so that corresponding APIs targeting the exchange type can be added in the future by qualifying method names with "Node", e.g. "GetJsonSchemaAsNode" and "OnSchemaNodeGenerated".

Yeah, I'm just curious if these are expected to be utilized still when the future version is implemented.  If not, is this considered acceptable bloat?  I'm not sure how this kind of thing is handled in .Net.

> That's changing in .NET 9 (for properties at least).

You're changing the default to serialize nulls?  That seems inefficient. Do you have an issue/PR for that?

> Yeah, I'm just curious if these are expected to be utilized still when the future version is implemented. If not, is this considered acceptable bloat? I'm not sure how this kind of thing is handled in .Net.

We can't ever remove APIs once they have been shipped, so it's expected that they would live on next to the future APIs that target an exchange type. It shouldn't be a huge issue size-wise, by that point they just be stub methods that convert to `JsonNode`. This is consistent with the variety of methods present in `JsonSerializer`, e.g. `Serialize`, `SerializeToNode`, `SerializerToElement`, `SerializeToBytes` etc.

> You're changing the default to serialize nulls? That seems inefficient. Do you have an issue/PR for that?

It's adding non-nullable reference type enforcement. See https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/100144

I think I'm interpreting things a bit wrong.

The default for the serializer is to skip null properties when writing, and the default for this is to generate a schema that allows null properties. 

My thinking was that these are related, but really the schema generation is related to serializer _reads_ where the default behavior is to allow nulls, which _does_ align with the default schema generation. 

Disallowing nulls in the schema aligns with the non-default behavior of disallowing nulls in deserialization, per that issue. 

I think we're good here.

> The default for the serializer is to skip null properties when writing

That's not the default behavior, unless `IgnoreNullValues`/`JsonIgnoreCondition` have been configured to do so. Obviously the exporter should be honoring whatever configuration is being used.

> but really the schema generation is related to serializer reads

That's an interesting observation. The prototype implementation is actually generating a schema that satisfies the union of serialization outputs and valid deserialization inputs. In other words, the schema of a property allows null if either the getter _or_ the setter are nullable (it's possible for the two to differ in annotation).

I think the API looks good.  Just reiterating that I'm still interested in the eventual logic behind it. 

What code constructs produce what schema constructs?  To be answered later, I assume, but it would be good to have this publicly documented, and I'd like to help guide these decisions.

> Just reiterating that I'm still interested in the eventual logic behind it.

Essentially it's just going to be a port of https://github.com/eiriktsarpalis/stj-schema-mapper, the [unit tests](https://github.com/eiriktsarpalis/stj-schema-mapper/blob/main/tests/JsonSchemaMapper.Tests/TestTypes.cs) should provide an idea of how it's meant to work.

review_comments: Remind me why we went with the "AsNode" suffix? Is that because we expect to have a schema type in the future and we want GetJsonSchema in the future to return that?
Correct.
RFC3339 vs ISO8601
Doesn't the `Uri` class also support IRIs?  If so, this can be `format: iri` or even `format: iri-reference` instead.  (IRI support is coming in the next JSON Schema release.  2020-12 uses URIs.)

According to [this document ](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.configuration.iriparsingelement?view=net-8.0) it's opt in behavior but I defer to @dotnet/ncl for a definitive answer.

I recognize that this is internal.  Supposing a `JsonSchema` type is exposed publicly in the future (i.e. JSON Schema has full support in .Net), are we okay with this class drastically changing to support extensibility?  If not should we call it `JsonSchemaExporterModel` or something?

> are we okay with this class drastically changing to support extensibility?

Yes. We are free to make changes to internal implementation detail without notice.
RFC3339 vs ISO8601
Referencing directly into keywords using pointers is not recommended

JSON Schema common practice is to extract subschemas into a `$defs` keyword.  It's generally considered a bad practice to `$ref` directly into other keywords using JSON Pointer.

This may not be supported by all validators.

I've updated the implementation so that `$ref`'s are only emitted for recursive types. My understanding is that a `$ref` is the only way such schemas can expressed (independent of whether they have been factored into a `$defs` section).

> My understanding is that a $ref is the only way such schemas can expressed

Correct.

> ... independent of whether they have been factored into a $defs section

_Technically_ correct, but again, not recommended best practice.

My concern is that other developers, seeing that .Net is doing this, will interpret it as a recommended approach (at least in .Net spheres) regardless of the fact that _JSON Schema_ recommends against it.

I strongly urge you to extract reference targets (that aren't the root schema) to `$defs`.

Alternatively, the `$anchor` or `$id` approach _as a default_ is acceptable.

Understood, at the same time I wanted to avoid shipping a baked in naming convention (since invariably that would involve either generating UUID's for every node in the type graph or leaking fully qualified type names to the schema). Using JSON pointer focuses on the structural aspect of the generated document, and users should be able to convert that to whatever naming convention they desire using the callback.

My main concern with the current approach is that JSON pointer currently only supports absolute paths, which causes it to break if composed inside other documents, putting the responsibility on users to fix it up. Because `$ref` is only generated for recursive types, a relative pointer would simply need to specify the depth of the recursive occurrence.

Also acceptable.  Though reviewers should be aware that the value of `$id` can be any URI, and the use of URLs has caused confusion as users tend to think of them as locators and expect the schema to be available at that location.

JSON Schema explicitly says that users shouldn't expect this to be the case, but no one reads the spec.
It would be neat for a custom converter to be able to explicitly specify the schema to use or for it to otherwise expose constraints on the JSON it will produce.  (eventually)
Absolutely! Such an addition is currently blocked by the lack of a public schema type.
Well, we should do that then. 😜
Using `$anchor` is an acceptable alternative.

FWIW the exporter itself never uses `$anchor` because I wanted to avoid having to unique generate identifiers for types. This particular tests validates that users can do that themselves via the provided callback mechanism.
Would be good to see this for sealed types as well.
The serializer doesn't disallow additional properties in sealed types. This can only be controlled via the `UnmappedMemberHandling` setting.

> The serializer doesn't disallow additional properties in sealed types.

Right. Wouldn't you want the schema to fail when the serialize does?  I'm saying that schema generation for sealed types should add `additionalProperties: false`.
I'm saying that the serializer doesn't fail in that case. Whether a type is sealed or not doesn't have any bearing on its serialization contract (since by default types don't support polymorphism).
JSON Schema's `date-time` is RFC3339, but .Net uses ISO8601.  ([Comparison](https://ijmacd.github.io/rfc3339-iso8601/))

I'm on the fence about this, since switching to a pattern would be trading off human readability for precision ([related conversation](https://github.com/eiriktsarpalis/stj-schema-mapper/pull/3#discussion_r1629168528)). I think we have to use a pattern for `DateTime` since it does use non-RFC3339 dates (for `DateTimeKind.Unspecified` values). For the case of `DateTimeOffset` the supported format is in the intersection of two formats, so using `date-time` feels like a natural choice (even if it means extending the converter to support other RFC3339 values).

What irks me with using patterns in this context is that it makes the schema less declarative. It's nontrivial to write a regex recognizing dates that doesn't admit some degree for false negatives, for instance using `\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}` to describe a date string admits invalid values such as `0000-01-01` and `9999-99-99`. 

Given that most date values serialized by STJ are recognized by the `date-time` format, I would be inclined to leave as-is for now, and we can iterate based on additional feedback.

Would this be analogous to JSON Pointer, where indexes are rendered as strings?  Would it (eventually, perhaps) be helpful to have a model for that (e.g. https://www.nuget.org/packages/JsonPointer.Net)?
It is something we would need to add at some point. In lieu of that exposing a span of breadcrumbs seemed like the safest design choice.

I suggest moving away from the term "path" as, when in context with JSON, suggests JSON Path.  (Think of `JsonNode.Path` property that actually returns a JSON Path syntax.)  Not sure what else to call this, though.
Hopefully the fact that it's a `ROS<string>` rather than a plain string should remove any confusion as to what this contains.
I don't see any protection against non-numeric values encoded in these strings.  Perhaps a `pattern` keyword could be warranted?
Added.
Is it possible to glean this from XML comments?  Does that make it into the JTI at all?  I expect it's available in the source generator.
I believe @captainsafia is doing this using a source generator in the OpenAPI side of things. It's not something that I think is in scope for the STJ generator though.
